exercises.title: U3 听力·对话 How the News Has Changed
exercises.speaker: uk_female
transcript: Lily: My grandpa says the news used to come only once a day. Is that true?
Tom: Yes. In the past, papers were delivered to the door every morning.
Lily: So people waited a whole day for the next story?
Tom: Exactly. And most interviews were done face to face back then.
Lily: How is it different now?
Tom: Now a story can be put online the moment it happens.
Lily: That's so fast! Do reporters still use paper?
Tom: Hardly ever. They write and edit almost everything on computers.
exercises.translation_cn: 莉莉问爷爷说过去新闻一天才来一次是否属实;汤姆说没错,过去报纸每天早上送到门口;人们要等一整天才有下一条;过去采访多是面对面;如今一条新闻一发生就能发到网上;记者几乎不用纸,都在电脑上写稿编辑。

questions.stem: How often did the news arrive in the past?
How were papers given to readers in the past?
options: Delivered to the door each morning.

questions.stem: How were most interviews done back then?
What can happen to a story now?
options: It must wait a whole day.
It can be put online the moment it happens.

questions.stem: What do reporters mainly use to work now?

exercises.title: U3 听力·短文 From Fishing Town to City
exercises.speaker: uk_female
transcript: Over forty years ago, a small fishing town stood by the southern sea.
People there made a living from fishing, and life was slow and quiet.
Then the town became a special economic zone, and everything began to change.
Roads were laid and tall buildings were put up year after year.
In just a few decades, the town grew into a busy modern city full of energy.
exercises.translation_cn: 四十多年前,南方海边有一座小渔镇;那里的人靠打鱼为生,生活缓慢而安静;后来小镇成了经济特区,一切开始改变;道路被铺设,高楼一年年盖起来;短短几十年,小镇就变成了一座充满活力的现代化城市。

questions.stem: What was the place like over forty years ago?
How did the people there make a living?
What change made things move quickly?
options: It became a special economic zone.

questions.stem: What was happening year after year?
options: Roads and tall buildings were going up.

questions.stem: What did the town become in a few decades?

exercises.title: U3 听力·对话 The Bookstore Lives On
exercises.speaker: uk_female
transcript: Anna: I can't believe the old bookstore is still here!
Ben: I know. The whole community worked together to save it.
Anna: And look — there's a café selling organic food now.
Ben: Yes, and the corner board has been replaced by a big screen.
Anna: People are writing their comments on it.
Ben: They even hold jazz concerts and poetry readings here.
Anna: It feels alive again. Who is in charge now?
Ben: A woman called Jennifer. She grew up in this very neighbourhood.
exercises.translation_cn: 安娜不敢相信老书店还在;本说是整个社区一起努力把它救了下来;现在还有卖有机食品的咖啡馆;角落里的木板被大屏幕取代,人们在上面写评论;店里甚至举办爵士音乐会和诗歌朗诵;书店重新焕发生机;现在的负责人是在这个社区长大的珍妮弗。

questions.stem: Why is the old bookstore still open?
options: The community worked together to save it.
It was never going to close.

questions.stem: What does the new café sell?
What has replaced the corner board?
What kind of events are held in the store now?
Who is in charge of the bookstore now?

exercises.title: U3 听力·短文 A Short History of Emojis
exercises.speaker: uk_female
transcript: The word emoji comes from Japanese and means picture character.
The first emojis appeared in Japan in 1999, with only about a hundred and seventy designs.
Today there are thousands of them, sorted into groups such as faces, animals and food.
People like emojis because they are quick to use and add feeling to a message.
Whatever we think, these little pictures are clearly here to stay.
exercises.translation_cn: emoji 一词来自日语,意为“图画文字”;最早的表情符号1999年出现在日本,只有约170种设计;如今已有成千上万种,分成表情、动物、食物等类别;人们喜欢表情符号,因为用起来快、还能给信息添情感;不管我们怎么看,这些小图画显然会一直存在下去。

questions.stem: Where does the word 'emoji' come from?
What does the word 'emoji' mean?
When did the first emojis appear?
Why do people like emojis, according to the passage?
options: They are quick and add feeling.

questions.stem: What does the speaker say about the future of emojis?

exercises.title: U3 听力·对话 The Vanished Phone Box
exercises.speaker: uk_female
transcript: Grandpa: When I was young, we used phone boxes on every street corner.
Mia: Phone boxes? What were they for?
Grandpa: To make calls when you were out. You put in coins and dialled.
Mia: But now everyone just uses a mobile phone.
Grandpa: That's right. Mobiles are far easier to carry and use.
Mia: So the phone boxes all disappeared?
Grandpa: Almost. People simply stopped needing them.
Mia: Times really do change, Grandpa!
exercises.translation_cn: 爷爷说他年轻时街角到处是电话亭;米娅问那是干什么的;爷爷说是在外面打电话用的,投币后拨号;可现在大家都用手机;手机更便于携带和使用;所以电话亭几乎都消失了;因为人们不再需要它们了;米娅感叹时代真的在变。

questions.stem: Where were phone boxes found when Grandpa was young?
What were phone boxes used for?
options: Making calls when you were out.

questions.stem: How did you pay to use a phone box?
Why did phone boxes almost disappear?
options: They were too expensive to build.

questions.stem: What has taken the place of phone boxes?

exercises.title: U3 听力·短文 Moving With the Times
exercises.speaker: uk_female
transcript: Here is a simple thought about change.
The world around us never stays still; tools, jobs and habits are always being made new.
Some people fear change and hold on to the past.
But change can also bring fresh chances and better ways of living.
The best idea is not to fight every change, but to learn from it and move forward with the times.
exercises.translation_cn: 关于“变化”有个简单的想法:我们周围的世界从不静止,工具、工作和习惯一直在更新;有些人害怕变化、紧抓过去;但变化也能带来新机会和更好的生活方式;最好的办法不是抗拒每一次变化,而是从中学习、随时代向前。

questions.stem: What does the passage say about the world around us?
What is always being made new?
How do some people react to change?
options: They welcome every bit of it.
They fear it and hold on to the past.

questions.stem: What can change also bring, according to the speaker?
options: Fresh chances and better ways of living.

questions.stem: What is the best idea about change?
options: To go back to the past.
To learn from it and move forward.
